fields.Front: What is the key difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
fields.Back: An image is a read-only, immutable template (layered filesystem + metadata) used to create containers. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with a thin writable layer added on top of the image's read-only layers.

fields.Front: What are Docker image layers, and why do they enable build caching?
fields.Back: Each Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY, etc.) produces a new read-only layer stacked on the previous ones. Docker caches each layer keyed by its instruction and inputs; if nothing changed, it reuses the cached layer instead of re-executing the instruction.

fields.Front: What does the FROM instruction do in a Dockerfile?
fields.Back: Specifies the base image the new image is built on, e.g. FROM node:20-alpine. It must be the first instruction (aside from an optional ARG before it).

fields.Front: What's the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?
fields.Back: RUN executes a command at build time and commits the result as a new image layer (e.g. installing packages). CMD specifies the default command a container runs at start time; it does not execute during the build.

fields.Front: What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
fields.Back: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable the container always runs. CMD supplies default arguments, which are overridden if arguments are passed to docker run. If both are set, CMD's values become ENTRYPOINT's default args.

fields.Front: What's the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?
fields.Back: COPY only copies files/directories from the build context into the image. ADD does that plus extra features: it auto-extracts local tar archives and can fetch remote URLs. Best practice: prefer COPY unless you specifically need ADD's extraction or URL behavior.

fields.Front: What does EXPOSE 8080 do in a Dockerfile, and what does it NOT do?
fields.Back: It documents that the container listens on port 8080 (metadata used by tools and docker run -P). It does NOT publish the port to the host — that requires -p on docker run.

fields.Front: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Node.js/TypeScript app that builds the code then ships only the compiled output.
fields.Back:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

fields.Front: What does docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx do?
fields.Back: Runs a container from the nginx image in detached mode (-d), maps host port 8080 to container port 80 (-p), and names the container web.

fields.Front: How do you build an image from a Dockerfile in the current directory and tag it myapp:1.0?
fields.Back: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . — the trailing . is the build context sent to the Docker daemon.

fields.Front: What does docker ps -a show that plain docker ps doesn't?
fields.Back: docker ps lists only running containers. docker ps -a lists all containers, including stopped/exited ones.

fields.Front: How do you get an interactive shell inside a running container?
fields.Back: docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash if available) — -i keeps STDIN open, -t allocates a TTY.

fields.Front: What's the difference between a named volume and a bind mount in Docker?
fields.Back: A named volume is created and managed by Docker in its own storage area (docker volume create), portable across hosts. A bind mount maps a specific host filesystem path directly into the container, tying the container to that host's layout.

fields.Front: By default, how do containers on the same user-defined Docker network reach each other?
fields.Back: By container name — Docker's embedded DNS resolves container names to their IPs on that network, so one container can reach another using its name as the hostname.

fields.Front: What does the -p 8080:80 flag mean in docker run -p 8080:80 myapp?
fields.Back: Maps host port 8080 to the container's port 80, in the form -p host:container, forwarding traffic that hits the host on 8080 into the container on port 80.
Lists files/paths (e.g. node_modules, .git) to exclude from the build context sent to the Docker daemon, keeping builds faster and images from accidentally including secrets or bloat.

fields.Front: Why does chaining multiple install commands into one RUN ... && ... reduce image size compared to separate RUN lines?
fields.Back: Each RUN creates a new layer; a separate update layer can go stale and any intermediate package caches persist in their own layer. Chaining into a single RUN (and cleaning caches in that same instruction) keeps it to one layer with no leftover cache data.

fields.Text: In a Dockerfile, once a layer's cache is invalidated (its instruction or inputs changed), {{c1::every layer after it}} must be rebuilt, even if their own instructions didn't change.
fields.Extra: This is why you order instructions from least- to most-frequently-changing (e.g. install deps before copying source).

fields.Text: A multi-stage Dockerfile uses multiple {{c1::FROM}} statements in one file so build artifacts from an earlier stage can be copied into a final, {{c2::smaller}} runtime image, leaving build-only tools and dependencies behind.
fields.Extra: Keeps compilers/dev dependencies out of the shipped image.

fields.Text: To shrink Docker image size: use a {{c1::minimal/alpine}} base image, {{c2::combine RUN commands}} to reduce layer count, use {{c3::multi-stage builds}} to drop build-only tools, and add a {{c4::.dockerignore}} to avoid copying unneeded files.
fields.Extra: All reduce the final image's footprint.
